messianic.name_of_god:
In Messianic Judaism, God's name is written YHVH, the four letters given in the Hebrew Scriptures. Following Jewish custom, many Messianic believers avoid pronouncing the name casually and say Hashem, which means the Name, out of reverence. Practice differs, and some congregations pronounce a form of the name in worship.

Messianic believers also use the Hebrew name Yeshua for Jesus, since it is the name by which he would have been known among his own people, and it means salvation. Using it is a way of stressing his Jewish identity and the Jewish roots of the faith. Most Messianic believers affirm that Yeshua is the Messiah and is one with God, though language about this varies among congregations.
messianic.sabbath:
Messianic believers commonly keep Shabbat, the seventh-day Sabbath, from Friday evening to Saturday evening. A typical observance includes lighting candles, a blessing over wine and bread, a family meal, rest from ordinary work, and congregational worship on Saturday with readings from the Torah and the Prophets.

Shabbat is treated as a joyful gift from God and as part of Jewish identity and practice which Jesus himself kept. Most Messianic believers do not teach that keeping it is required for salvation, and they generally do not judge other Christians who worship on Sunday. How strictly the day is observed varies from one congregation and family to another.
messianic.food_laws:
Many Messianic Jews and other Messianic believers choose to keep kashrut, the biblical food laws as understood in Jewish tradition, such as avoiding pork and shellfish and keeping meat and dairy apart. For them it expresses Jewish identity, obedience to God's instruction and solidarity with the Jewish people.

Messianic believers generally teach that this is a matter of practice and conscience, not a requirement for salvation, and that Gentile believers are not bound to it. They read New Testament passages about food in different ways, and some congregations keep kosher strictly, others partly, and others not at all. What they share is the conviction that faith in Yeshua does not remove Jewish believers from Jewish life and practice.
